Admission pins a seat to one ringing station's re-sighting ledger. The applicant holds a permit earned over 300 supervised hours across two years, and proves it with birds it pigment-marked: a patch legible at forty metres, enough to name one sparrow without recapture. Weekly the node pulls photos from the public re-sighting pool, wants an observer beyond the ringer, and checks the telemetry signal of a tagged bird to confirm the site is real ground.

A kit is 90 dollars, a receiver 1,800, but hours are the wall: 50 stations need 15,000 supervised hours, eight years of weekends.
